source: Heuristic Test Strategy Model (HTSM) v6.3 by James Bach: product elements (SFDIPOT), quality criteria, general test techniques, and the FEW HICCUPPS consistency oracles (Michael Bolton). Descriptions are ours.

heuristics.name: Structure
heuristics.description: What does the product actually consist of, physically, code, executables and routines, integral hardware, independently-running services/servers, non-executable files (text, sample data, help files), and collateral (documents, web pages, packaging, license agreements)? Are all these pieces individually testable and accounted for?
heuristics.apply: List the pieces the product is made of (pages, services, files, docs) and check each one can be reached and tested.

heuristics.name: Function
heuristics.description: What does this system's operations actually DO, semantically, not the literal field names, but the real-world actions/effects (e.g. 'authorizes and charges a payment method', 'applies tiered bulk pricing', 'tracks a running balance').
heuristics.apply: Write down what each operation really does for a user, then test that meaning rather than the field names.

heuristics.name: Data
heuristics.description: What KINDS of data does this system handle, financial values, PII-adjacent fields, categorical/enum fields, temporal fields, etc.? Focus on the nature and sensitivity of the data itself, not the operations performed on it.
heuristics.apply: List the kinds of data the product takes in and gives out, then give each kind its own tests.

heuristics.name: Interfaces
heuristics.description: Through what conduits is the product accessed or expressed, user interfaces (displays, buttons, fields), system interfaces (logs, other programs, disk, network), APIs/SDKs for third-party developers, and import/export functions that package or interpret data for other products?
heuristics.apply: List every way in and out of the product (screens, APIs, imports, exports) and test each one.

heuristics.name: Platform
heuristics.description: What does the product depend on that's outside the project itself, external hardware/software required or optional for it to work, embedded components/libraries produced elsewhere, and the resource footprint (memory, filehandles) it consumes in that environment?
heuristics.apply: List what the product depends on outside itself (browser, OS, services) and vary or remove each.

heuristics.name: Operations
heuristics.description: What experiences do real users actually have with the product, who are the different kinds of users, what's their physical/environmental context, and what does common, uncommon, extreme, and disfavored (careless, malicious, mistaken) use of it look like?
heuristics.apply: Describe who uses the product and how, then test the common, the rare and the careless ways of using it.

heuristics.name: Time
heuristics.description: How does the product relate to time, time-related data (timeouts, timezones, holidays, warranty periods), timing relationships between input and output, pacing (fast/slow/bursty input), and concurrency (multiple things happening at once)?
heuristics.apply: Look for anything that depends on time (timeouts, dates, time zones, order of events) and change it.

heuristics.name: Capability
heuristics.description: Can it perform the required functions? Sufficiency, does it have all the capabilities necessary for its purpose, and correctness, can it function as intended and produce output that's acceptably accurate?
heuristics.apply: Check the product can actually do each thing it's for, completely and correctly.

heuristics.name: Reliability
heuristics.description: Will it work well and resist failure in all required situations, robustness (no degradation over time or under reasonable stress), error handling (graceful failure and recovery from bad data or conditions), data integrity (protection from loss or corruption), and safety (won't harm life or property even under failure)?
heuristics.apply: Use it for longer, with bad input and in odd situations, and watch for failures and degradation.

heuristics.name: Usability
heuristics.description: How easy is it for a real user to use, learnability (can the intended user rapidly master its operation), operability (minimum effort and fuss to operate day-to-day), and accessibility (meets accessibility standards and platform accessibility features)?
heuristics.apply: Try each task as a new user would and note where it's slow to learn, confusing or error-prone.

heuristics.name: Charisma
heuristics.description: How appealing is the product, aesthetics (appeals to the senses), uniqueness (new or special in some way), entrancement (users get hooked, have fun, or stay engaged), and image (projects the desired impression of quality)?
heuristics.apply: Note whether the product looks and feels appealing and trustworthy, not just whether it works.

heuristics.name: Security
heuristics.description: How well is it protected against unauthorized use or intrusion, authentication (verifying who a user is), authorization (rights granted to authenticated users at varying privilege levels), privacy (protecting customer/employee data from unauthorized people), and security holes (ways the system fails to enforce security, including via social engineering)?
heuristics.apply: Check that only the right people can see and do what they should, and that data stays protected.

heuristics.name: Scalability
heuristics.description: How well does the deployment of the product scale up or down, in users, data volume, load, or geographic distribution?
heuristics.apply: Grow the number of users, the amount of data or the load, and watch how the product copes.

heuristics.name: Compatibility
heuristics.description: How well does it work with external components and configurations, other applications, particular operating systems, particular hardware, earlier versions of itself (backward compatibility), and does it avoid unnecessarily hogging memory, storage, or other shared resources?
heuristics.apply: Run it with other browsers, systems, settings and neighbouring software it has to work with.

heuristics.name: Performance
heuristics.description: How speedy and responsive is it, under normal and under adverse conditions?
heuristics.apply: Time the main actions, under normal load and under heavy load, and compare with what users would accept.

heuristics.name: Installability
heuristics.description: How easily can it be installed onto its target platform(s), does it recognize missing or insufficient system requirements, what parts of the system does installation affect and where are files/resources stored, is uninstallation clean, can upgrades/patches be applied easily while respecting existing configuration, and who or what schedule handles installation?
heuristics.apply: Install, upgrade and uninstall it, including on a system that's missing something it needs.

heuristics.name: Development
heuristics.description: How well can we create, test, and modify it, supportability (economical to support users), testability (how effectively it can be tested), maintainability (economical to build, fix, or enhance), portability (economical to port or reuse elsewhere), and localizability (economical to adapt for other places)?
heuristics.apply: Judge how easy the product is to test, support and change: logs, error messages, configurability.

heuristics.name: Function Testing
heuristics.description: Test what it can do: identify the product's functions and subfunctions, determine how you'd know if a function is capable of working, test each one individually, and confirm it does what it's supposed to and not what it isn't supposed to do.
heuristics.apply: List the functions and subfunctions, decide how you'd know each works, and test them one at a time.

heuristics.name: Claims Testing
heuristics.description: Challenge every claim: identify reference materials with claims about the product (SLAs, EULAs, ads, specs, help text, manuals), analyze and clarify vague claims, test each one, and, if testing from an explicit spec, expect spec and product to be brought into alignment. Related to but distinct from the 'claims' FEW-HICCUPPS oracle below, that oracle judges whether a documented claim holds true for a given result, while this technique is the procedural approach of hunting down and testing every claim the product makes.
heuristics.apply: Collect every claim the docs, help or marketing make, and test each one literally.

heuristics.name: Domain Testing
heuristics.description: Partition the data: look at data the product processes (including outputs, not just inputs), decide which specific values to test with (boundary, typical, convenient, invalid, best-representative), consider combinations worth testing together, and use inputs that force the whole range of possible outputs to occur.
heuristics.apply: Split each input and output into groups that should behave alike, then test one value per group and the edges.

heuristics.name: User Testing
heuristics.description: Involve the users: identify categories or roles of users, determine what each does and values (use cases), get real user data or logs or bring real users in, otherwise systematically simulate a user carefully, and favor a variety of users/roles over just one.
heuristics.apply: Work through the product as each kind of user would, with their goals and habits.

heuristics.name: Stress Testing
heuristics.description: Overwhelm the product: look for sub-systems or functions vulnerable to overload or breakage under challenging data or constrained resources, then select or generate challenging conditions to test with (large or complex data, high loads, long runs, many test cases, low memory).
heuristics.apply: Push the parts most likely to break (big inputs, many requests, little memory) past normal limits.

heuristics.name: Risk Testing
heuristics.description: Imagine a problem, then look for it: what kinds of problems could the product have, which matter most, how would you detect them if present, and design tests specifically to reveal them, consulting experts, design docs, past bug reports, or risk heuristics as needed.
heuristics.apply: Imagine a specific problem the product could have, then design a test that would reveal it.

heuristics.name: Flow Testing
heuristics.description: Do one thing after another: perform multiple activities connected end-to-end (e.g. tours through a state model) without resetting the system between actions, varying timing and sequencing, and trying parallel threads.
heuristics.apply: Do several actions in a row without resetting, so each one starts from what the last one left.

heuristics.name: Tool-Supported Testing
heuristics.description: Use tools to make testers more powerful: look for or develop tools that perform many actions or checks, partially automate test coverage, partially automate oracles, detect changes automatically, or generate test data automatically.
heuristics.apply: Use a tool to do many actions or checks a person couldn't, such as many inputs or long runs.

heuristics.name: Scenario Testing
heuristics.description: Test to a compelling story: think about everything going on around the product, design tests involving meaningful and complex interactions with it, where a good scenario is a compelling story of how someone who matters might do something that matters with the product.
heuristics.apply: Write a realistic story of someone using the product for a real goal, and follow it through.

heuristics.name: Claims
heuristics.description: What EXPLICIT, documented claims does the spec make that can be mechanically checked against any real response? (e.g. 'decline_reason must be one of these N documented values', 'credits_purchased must be 0 if declined').
heuristics.apply: Compare what you see with what the spec, docs or help say should happen.

heuristics.name: Comparable products
heuristics.description: Does this system belong to a recognizable category of real-world systems? If so, what conventions or behaviors do systems in that category typically get right (or wrong) that this system should be checked against, even if never explicitly documented?
heuristics.apply: Compare the behaviour with similar products users already know, and question differences.

heuristics.name: Dumb user
heuristics.description: Would a naive user find this confusing or wrong, regardless of whether it's technically spec-compliant? Judge from the perspective of someone with no special knowledge of the system's internals or documentation.
heuristics.apply: Ask whether an ordinary user would find the result confusing or wrong, even if it matches the spec.

heuristics.name: Statistical/trend
heuristics.description: Does this deviate from the system's own past behavior, latency drift, error-rate creep, or other trends observable only by comparing against prior runs or history? Needs accumulated data across runs to be meaningful; not useful on a single, first-time pass.
heuristics.apply: Compare with how this product behaved before: slower, more errors, or different results is a warning sign.

heuristics.name: Familiarity
heuristics.description: Is this a kind of problem you've seen in other products? Known bug patterns are worth checking for on purpose.
heuristics.apply: Pick a problem common in this kind of product (lost form data, stale totals) and look for it here.

heuristics.name: Explainability
heuristics.description: Can you explain what the product just did? Behaviour nobody can explain is worth reporting even if it isn't clearly wrong.
heuristics.apply: After each surprising result, try to explain it in one sentence; if you can't, note it as a finding.

heuristics.name: World
heuristics.description: Does the product agree with how the real world works: dates, units, addresses, names, arithmetic?
heuristics.apply: Check shown facts against the real world, such as valid dates, correct sums and realistic units.

heuristics.name: Image
heuristics.description: Does the behaviour fit the image the organisation wants? Rude messages, sloppy text or odd visuals hurt it.
heuristics.apply: Read messages and labels as a customer would, looking for anything embarrassing or careless.

heuristics.name: Purpose
heuristics.description: Does the behaviour serve what the product is for, and what the user is trying to do?
heuristics.apply: For each result, ask whether it helps the user reach their goal or gets in the way.

heuristics.name: Statutes and standards
heuristics.description: Does the product follow the laws, regulations and standards that apply to it, such as accessibility or privacy rules?
heuristics.apply: Name the standards that apply (WCAG, privacy law, payment rules) and check the product against them.
